payload.question_text: An analyst is choosing semantic-embedding capabilities for a text-analysis workflow. Which tasks can the system support? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Embeddings can identify sentences central to overall meaning. Those existing sentences can be selected as a summary.
Punctuation removal is a preprocessing operation. It is not a semantic embedding application.
options.better_fit: Use punctuation removal when normalizing text before analysis.

feedback.intrinsic: Text would be prepared but no meaning-based task would be completed.
feedback.instructional: Embeddings support semantic tasks such as summarization and entity recognition.

options.rationale: Word vectors can be compared with a document vector. Semantically central words can become keywords.
Token embeddings in context can support recognizing entities. Context helps distinguish entity roles.

payload.explanation: Correct. Semantic embeddings can support summarization, keywords, and entity recognition.

payload.question_text: What do semantic language models encode?

options.rationale: Frequency counts measure occurrence, not relationships in meaning. They do not produce semantic token representations.
options.better_fit: Use frequency counts when identifying commonly occurring terms.

feedback.intrinsic: Related words would remain separate counts.
feedback.instructional: Semantic models represent relationships in meaning, not only frequency.

options.rationale: Semantic language models encode relationships among language tokens. Those relationships enable machines to work with meaning.
Grammatical labels identify roles such as noun or verb. They do not encode semantic relationships between tokens.
options.better_fit: Use POS tagging when a token's grammatical category is needed.

feedback.intrinsic: You would get a grammar label instead of semantic relationships.
feedback.instructional: Semantic models focus on meaning relationships.

options.rationale: Graph edges connect nodes in a TextRank-style graph. Semantic language models encode token relationships as vectors.
options.better_fit: Use sentence-graph edges when ranking sentences for extractive summarization.

feedback.intrinsic: You would select a graph structure rather than a token representation.
feedback.instructional: Graphs rank nodes; semantic models encode token meaning.

payload.explanation: Correct. These models encode relationships between language tokens.

payload.question_text: An analyst selects a semantic keyword-extraction method for a document. The method finds key terms by comparing only how often each word appears.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Important but less frequent meaning-bearing terms could be missed.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Semantic extraction uses vector relationships, not frequency alone.

payload.explanation: Correct. Semantic keyword extraction compares word vectors with a document representation.

payload.question_text: Word2Vec and GloVe represent tokens as dense vectors with many numeric dimensions.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The numeric representation would be overlooked.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Word2Vec and GloVe use dense vectors with many dimensions.

payload.explanation: Correct. Their representations are dense, multi-dimensional numeric vectors.

payload.question_text: Which statements describe an embedding? Select all that apply.

options.text: It is a multi-valued numeric vector.
options.rationale: An embedding contains multiple numeric values. Together they represent a language token.
Embeddings depend on numeric dimensions. Those values determine vector relationships.
options.better_fit: Use a simple category label when no vector representation is needed.

feedback.intrinsic: There would be no vector orientation to compare.
feedback.instructional: Embeddings are numeric and multi-dimensional.

options.text: It represents a token in multidimensional space.
options.rationale: A vector can be treated as a point in multidimensional space. Embeddings use this representation for tokens.

options.text: It is only a count of occurrences.
options.rationale: Occurrence counts are frequency features. An embedding is a vector representation rather than a count.
options.better_fit: Use word counts in bag-of-words feature extraction.

feedback.intrinsic: Meaning relationships would not be represented.
feedback.instructional: Keep count-based features separate from embeddings.

payload.explanation: Correct. An embedding is a numeric vector representing a token.

payload.question_text: Which parts appear in the cosine similarity formula? Select all that apply.

options.text: The dot product of A and B
options.rationale: The dot product is the numerator of the formula. It combines the two vectors' dimensions.
The magnitude of A is in the denominator. It normalizes the directional comparison.
The magnitude of B is also in the denominator. Both magnitudes are required.
Document count is used by inverse document frequency. Cosine similarity uses two vectors, their dot product, and magnitudes.
options.better_fit: Use document count when calculating inverse document frequency.

feedback.intrinsic: A corpus-wide count would be mixed into a two-vector calculation.
feedback.instructional: Cosine similarity does not use a document count.

payload.explanation: Correct. The formula uses a dot product and both vector magnitudes.

payload.question_text: Semantically similar words usually have vectors pointing in very different directions.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Related words would be placed as unrelated directions.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Semantic similarity is generally reflected by similar, not very different, directions.

payload.explanation: Correct. Similar meanings tend to have similar vector orientations.

payload.question_text: An engineer is configuring attention for a language model. What does attention calculate for a token?

options.rationale: Occurrence frequency is a count-based feature. Attention calculates contextual influence.
options.better_fit: Use frequency analysis to count token occurrences.

feedback.intrinsic: Changing meaning across contexts would be missed.
feedback.instructional: Attention focuses on surrounding-token influence.

options.rationale: POS tagging assigns grammatical categories. Attention builds a context-aware representation.
options.better_fit: Use POS tagging to label nouns, verbs, or adjectives.

feedback.intrinsic: You would obtain a grammar label instead of a contextual representation.
feedback.instructional: Attention is about contextual influence.

options.rationale: Graph edge counts concern network relationships. Attention measures the influence of surrounding tokens.
options.better_fit: Use graph edges when ranking connected nodes in TextRank.

feedback.intrinsic: You would rank graph connections rather than capture context.
feedback.instructional: Attention shapes token representations using context.

options.rationale: Attention calculates the influence of surrounding tokens. That influence shapes a contextualized representation.

payload.explanation: Correct. Attention evaluates how nearby tokens influence a representation.

payload.question_text: A high cosine similarity means two vectors have similar orientations.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Aligned vectors would be treated as unrelated.

payload.explanation: Correct. A high score signals similar vector directions.

payload.question_text: An engineer uses the supplied animal embeddings in a semantic model. Which vector operations are shown by the examples? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Adding young transforms dog toward puppy. It represents an adult-to-young relationship.
The same transformation maps cat toward kitten. The relationship is encoded as vector arithmetic.
Tree does not represent the young transformation. The examples use young to connect adult and young animals.
options.better_fit: Use tree when comparing its similarity with animal words.

feedback.intrinsic: The adult-to-young relationship would be lost.
feedback.instructional: Use young as the semantic transformation vector.

options.rationale: Subtracting young reverses the transformation. It returns from puppy toward dog.

payload.explanation: Correct. Adding or subtracting young moves between adult and young-animal relationships.

payload.question_text: Contextualized embeddings let a token's representation reflect its surrounding context.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Nearby words would be treated as irrelevant.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Contextualized embeddings reflect context through attention.

payload.explanation: Correct. Attention uses surrounding tokens to shape the representation.

payload.question_text: Vector arithmetic requires the resulting vector to exactly match a word vector in real systems.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Useful near matches could be rejected.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Exact matches are uncommon; retrieve the closest vector instead.

payload.explanation: Correct. Real systems usually retrieve the closest vector.

evidence.statement: All marked answers and explanations align with the supplied source: embeddings support extractive summarization, keyword extraction, and named entity recognition; semantic models encode token relationships; cosine similarity uses a dot product and both magnitudes; and vector arithmetic examples match the source.

Each item has a clearly indicated answer, and the alternatives do not create a competing defensible answer under the stated instructions; for example, the cosine formula item explicitly distinguishes vector magnitudes from document-count terminology.

Distractors are generally credible concept confusions rather than random choices, including frequency analysis versus semantic modeling, POS tagging versus attention, TextRank versus embeddings, and IDF versus cosine similarity.

Wrong choices are labeled with realistic misconceptions and paired with corrective explanations, such as treating embeddings as occurrence counts, treating attention as POS tagging, or assuming vector arithmetic requires exact matches.

The sequence covers foundational content but begins with semantic-model applications before establishing embeddings and vector representations, then revisits attention and cosine similarity after related concepts have already appeared. A more coherent progression would establish embeddings, orientation, similarity, attention, applications, and arithmetic before consolidation checks.

The session uses only multiple-choice and true/false mechanics, with several adjacent same-mechanic pairs and a true/false pair at the end. The alternation is serviceable but offers limited rhythm variation.
Prompt forms vary between which-task, what-definition, select-all, and true/false statements, but several stems repeat the same patterns, especially Which... and What... formulations.

The items are almost entirely decontextualized definition or assertion checks; they do not ask learners to make a realistic text-analysis, modeling, or engineering decision. Examples include selecting supported embedding tasks, identifying what attention calculates, and recognizing vector equations.

Feedback usually identifies the governing distinction and a next step, such as separating preprocessing from embedding applications, using vector relationships for semantic extraction, and retrieving the closest vector when exact matches are uncommon.

The Level 1 unit is appropriately focused on recognition and basic understanding, with a small amount of formula and vector-operation interpretation. The difficulty is suitable for a new learner, though the session offers limited application beyond recall.

Terms such as embeddings, semantic models, contextualized embeddings, attention, cosine similarity, vector orientation, and vector arithmetic are used consistently with the source and across the session.
The session is correct, internally consistent, and well supported by feedback, but its exact sequence is less coherent than it could be and provides little realistic task context or mechanic variety.

largest_gap.summary: The session lacks credible text-analysis or modeling scenarios and relies almost entirely on abstract recall prompts.

evidence.statement: Items ask learners to identify definitions, formulas, or vector equations without placing them in a realistic analyst, developer, or model-use decision; this is visible in the task-selection, attention, and vector-operation prompts.

largest_gap.repair_instruction: Reframe only the question_text of these four items as short, source-bounded analyst or engineer tasks using the existing answer choices and correct answers; preserve question_type exactly and do not introduce claims beyond the supplied source.

result.concise_summary: The artifact is highly source-faithful, unambiguous, and diagnostically strong, with useful feedback and consistent terminology. Its main weakness is that it is abstract rather than scenario-based; progression and mechanic rhythm are also moderate weaknesses. The proposed item-scoped prompt reframing is safe and source-bounded.

evidence.statement: All keyed answers and explanatory claims are supported by the supplied source: embeddings support extractive summarization, keyword extraction, and named entity recognition; semantic models encode token relationships; Word2Vec/GloVe use dense multidimensional vectors; attention uses surrounding-token influence; and the vector-arithmetic examples and closest-vector caveat are reproduced faithfully.

Each item has a determinable key under its instructions. The multi-select items identify exactly the source-supported statements, while the true/false items make single propositions whose truth values follow directly from the source.

Distractors are generally credible category confusions rather than random choices: frequency analysis, POS tagging, TextRank, IDF, normalization, bag-of-words, and unrelated vectors are all concepts discussed in the source but distinct from the target concept.

Wrong choices and incorrect-answer feedback diagnose realistic confusions between semantic embeddings and frequency counts, POS tags, TextRank graphs, TF-IDF document counts, normalization, bag-of-words, and unrelated vector arithmetic.

The exact sequence covers a sensible concept arc from semantic-model applications through token relationships, vectors, orientation, attention, cosine similarity, and vector arithmetic. However, it introduces applications before establishing the underlying embedding representation and interleaves repeated rung-1 and rung-2 checks, so the progression is coherent but not optimally scaffolded.

The session alternates multiple-choice and true/false mechanics across the ordered items, avoiding long uninterrupted runs of one mechanic; the sequence contains six multiple-choice items and six true/false items.

Prompt stems vary across definitional, selection, analyst, engineer, and assertion formats, but several items repeatedly use closely related analyst/engineer framing and multiple prompts use 'Which...' or declarative true/false constructions.

Analyst and engineer contexts are credible for semantic text-analysis work, including choosing capabilities, configuring attention, and using supplied embeddings. The remaining definition and assertion items are appropriate conceptual checks rather than implausible scenarios.

Correct-answer explanations state the governing concept, and incorrect options generally include intrinsic impact, instructional correction, and a better-fit source concept. The true/false feedback likewise explains the misconception and the corrective principle.

The items are mostly remembering and understanding checks, matching a Level 1 unit whose objective is to use embeddings and vector relationships to explain semantic text analysis; the vector-arithmetic and cosine items add modest application without exceeding the stated level.

Core terms are used consistently with the source, including semantic embeddings, token relationships, dense vectors, contextualized embeddings, attention, cosine similarity, and vector arithmetic. Distinct preprocessing and statistical terms are explicitly separated from embedding concepts.

The 12-item sequence is factually reliable, balanced between multiple-choice and true/false, and provides corrective feedback. Its main learner-experience limitation is repetitive recognition-level checking and a somewhat suboptimal order that places applications before foundational representation concepts.

largest_gap.summary: The sequence is coherent but foundational concepts are introduced after an applications-first opening, and repeated rung-1/rung-2 checks interleave rather than building in a clean scaffold.

evidence.statement: The first item asks learners to select embedding-supported applications before the session defines what semantic language models encode and what an embedding is; later items then revisit the same concepts through adjacent true/false checks.

largest_gap.repair_instruction: Reorder the existing item objects so foundational concepts precede applications and follow-up checks, for example placing semantic language models and embeddings before semantic-model applications, while preserving every item object and payload unchanged.

result.concise_summary: The challenger is source-faithful, unambiguous, well-termed, and feedback-rich, with credible distractors and varied mechanics. The largest safe improvement is session-level reordering to strengthen foundational cognitive scaffolding.
